--- title: "Classification performance measures" description: "Presence can be scored on the calls at one threshold, on how well the probabilities rank the stations, or on the probabilities themselves. F1 cannot tell a model from calling every station present, ROC AUC scores the ranking at every threshold, and log loss checks that the probabilities can be read as chances." order: 4 categories: [validation, metrics, classification] --- ## Presence can be scored in three ways [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) scored its calls of present or absent by accuracy, and [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#three-measures-count-misses-and-false-alarms-apart) added sensitivity, specificity and precision. All four count the calls at one threshold. A model that predicts presence gives more than calls, though: it gives a probability for every station, which ranks the stations from most to least likely to hold the species. So there are three things to score: the **calls** at one threshold, the **ranking** the probabilities make, and the **probabilities** themselves. This page adds the measures most used in machine learning for each, and shows that a model can look good on one and poor on another. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Measures at one threshold count the calls Three summaries of the calls are common in machine learning. Each turns the four counts at a threshold into one number: true presences, false alarms, misses and true absences, often set out as a two-by-two table called the **confusion matrix**. | Measure | What it is | A rule that calls every station present scores | | --- | --- | --- | | **Accuracy** | the share of calls that are right | the share of stations with the species | | **F1** | an average of precision and sensitivity, pulled towards the lower of the two | close to 1 when presence is common | | **Balanced accuracy** | the average of sensitivity and specificity | 0.5 | | **MCC**, the Matthews correlation coefficient | the correlation between the calls and the truth, from −1 to 1 | nothing: its calls never vary, so there is no correlation to work out | F1 is built from precision and sensitivity, and neither counts the **true absences**, the absent stations called absent. F1 suits a search for something rare, where the absences are many and uninteresting. Balanced accuracy and MCC count every cell, and treat presence and absence alike. ## ROC AUC scores the ranking at every threshold [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd#upsampling-gives-the-same-answers-as-a-lower-threshold) drew a model's sensitivity against its specificity at every threshold. That curve is the **ROC curve** (receiver operating characteristic, a name from radar). The area under it, the **ROC AUC**, sums up the whole curve in one number, so models can be compared before a threshold is chosen. It is also the share of pairs, one station with the species and one without, in which the station with the species gets the higher probability. A ROC AUC of 1 ranks every station with the species above every station without it; 0.5 is no better than ranking at random. ROC AUC depends only on the order of the probabilities. Raising every probability, or squeezing them all towards 0.5, leaves the order and the ROC AUC unchanged. ## Log loss scores the probabilities themselves **Log loss**, from [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#counts-and-presence-have-their-own-losses), charges each station for the probability the model gave to what happened: little for a high probability of presence where the species was found, a lot for a confident call that turned out wrong. Lower is better. It rewards probabilities that are **spread out**, high where the species is and low where it is not, and **calibrated**: of the stations given 0.8, about 8 in 10 hold the species. ROC AUC sees only the first of these. ::: {.diagram} ![ROC AUC and log loss on two sets of eight probabilities. Left, every station with the species is ranked above every station without it, but all eight probabilities are high: ROC AUC is perfect, and log loss charges heavily for the absent stations called likely. Right, one pair is in the wrong order, but the probabilities sit near the truth: ROC AUC is a little lower and log loss much lower. The two measures rank the two sets in opposite orders.](img/auc-and-log-loss.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each with four stations where the species is present, drawn filled, and four where it is absent, drawn open, placed along an axis of predicted probability of presence from 0 to 1. Left, right order, too sure of presence: the present stations sit at 0.85 and above, the absent ones between 0.6 and 0.8; ROC AUC 1.00, log loss 0.66. Right, some order wrong, honest: the present stations sit between 0.4 and 0.9 and the absent ones between 0.1 and 0.6, so one absent station is ranked above one present station; ROC AUC 0.94, log loss 0.40. A note says ROC AUC is the share of present–absent pairs in which the present station has the higher probability, and log loss charges each station for the probability it gave to what happened, most for a confident miss."} ::: ## Worked example The outcome is `present`, whether the species was caught at a station at all. Three models predict it: - **Predicting the share present**: every station gets the share of the fitted stations with the species. It has no skill, and the other two should beat it. - **Logistic regression**, from [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd), with each input entered as a straight line in the log-odds. - **Random forest**, from [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd). For presence, each tree gives the share of stations with the species in the leaf a station falls in, and the forest averages those shares into a probability. As on [Regression performance measures](regression-metrics.qmd), every model is cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites, and each measure is worked out from the pooled out-of-fold probabilities. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() set.seed(61) folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10) inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") presence_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(inputs, "present"), data = survey) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("classification") models <- list( "Predicting the share present" = null_model(mode = "classification"), "Logistic regression" = logistic_reg(), "Random forest" = forest ) # every station's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) { fit_resamples(workflow(presence_recipe, model), folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> arrange(.row) |> pull(.pred_yes) }) predictions <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |> mutate(present = survey$present) |> pivot_longer(-present, names_to = "model", values_to = "probability") |> mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) tibble(stations = nrow(survey), `share present` = mean(survey$present == "yes"), `outcome levels` = str_flatten(levels(survey$present), ", ")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| share present|outcome levels | |--------:|-------------:|:--------------| | 800| 0.775|yes, no |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score, f1_score, log_loss, matthews_corrcoef, roc_auc_score, roc_curve) from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() present = (survey["present"] == "yes").to_numpy() folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61) inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical] def with_inputs(model): recipe = ColumnTransformer([ # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]) models = { "Predicting the share present": DummyClassifier(strategy="prior"), "Logistic regression": LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000), # as ranger does for probabilities: a few inputs at each question, # and no split of a leaf with fewer than 10 stations "Random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_split=10, random_state=1), } # every station's out-of-fold probability of presence, in the survey's order; # column 1 of predict_proba is the probability of True out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], present, cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"], method="predict_proba")[:, 1] for name, model in models.items()} predictions = (pd.DataFrame(out_of_fold).assign(present=present) .melt(id_vars="present", var_name="model", value_name="probability")) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "share present": [present.mean()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | share present | |-----------:|----------------:| | 800 | 0.775 | ::: ::: ::: The species was caught at 78% of the 800 stations, so presence is the common answer here. yardstick treats the first level of the outcome as the event a measure is about, and `present` lists `yes` first, so every measure below is about presence. In scikit-learn the outcome is `True` for presence, which its measures take as the event by default. ### F1 cannot tell the models from calling every station present At the default threshold of 0.5, predicting the share present calls every station present, since it gives every station a probability near 0.78. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} calls <- predictions |> mutate(called = factor(if_else(probability >= 0.5, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no"))) at_threshold <- calls |> summarise(`true absences` = sum(called == "no" & present == "no"), accuracy = accuracy_vec(present, called), F1 = f_meas_vec(present, called), `balanced accuracy` = bal_accuracy_vec(present, called), # NA where the calls never vary MCC = suppressWarnings(mcc_vec(present, called)), .by = model) at_threshold |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | true absences| accuracy| F1| balanced accuracy| MCC| |:----------------------------|-------------:|--------:|-----:|-----------------:|-----:| |Predicting the share present | 0| 0.775| 0.873| 0.500| NA| |Logistic regression | 13| 0.782| 0.876| 0.530| 0.163| |Random forest | 39| 0.785| 0.873| 0.583| 0.246|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def at_threshold(g, threshold=0.5): called = g.probability >= threshold return pd.Series({ "true absences": int((~called & ~g.present).sum()), "accuracy": accuracy_score(g.present, called), "F1": f1_score(g.present, called), "balanced accuracy": balanced_accuracy_score(g.present, called), # scikit-learn gives 0 where the calls never vary "MCC": matthews_corrcoef(g.present, called), }) calls = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False) .apply(at_threshold, include_groups=False).reset_index()) calls.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | true absences | accuracy | F1 | balanced accuracy | MCC | |:-----------------------------|----------------:|-----------:|------:|--------------------:|------:| | Predicting the share present | 0 | 0.775 | 0.873 | 0.5 | 0 | | Logistic regression | 12 | 0.778 | 0.873 | 0.525 | 0.129 | | Random forest | 41 | 0.784 | 0.871 | 0.586 | 0.248 | ::: ::: ::: Accuracy and F1 barely move. The rule that calls every station present has an F1 of 0.873, and neither model is more than 0.002 away from it. The models differ in the true absences: of the 180 stations without the species, logistic regression called 13 absent and the random forest 39. F1 never counts those stations, so it cannot see the difference. Balanced accuracy and MCC can. Balanced accuracy puts the rule at 0.500, logistic regression at 0.530 and the forest at 0.583, and MCC gives 0.163 and 0.246. MCC cannot be worked out for the rule: yardstick reports it as missing, and scikit-learn as 0, the value for calls unrelated to the truth. Both models are only a little better than the rule at this threshold, and the forest is the better of the two. ### The forest ranks the stations better Predicting the share present is left out here. Within a fold it gives every station the same probability, so it ranks nothing. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ranked <- filter(predictions, model != rule) |> mutate(model = fct_drop(model)) ranked |> summarise(`ROC AUC` = round(roc_auc_vec(present, probability), 3), .by = model) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | ROC AUC| |:-------------------|-------:| |Logistic regression | 0.671| |Random forest | 0.723|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} ranked = predictions[predictions["model"] != "Predicting the share present"] (ranked.groupby("model", sort=False) .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({"ROC AUC": roc_auc_score(g.present, g.probability)}), include_groups=False) .reset_index().round(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | ROC AUC | |:--------------------|----------:| | Logistic regression | 0.65 | | Random forest | 0.703 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(curves, aes(specificity, sensitivity, colour = model)) + geom_abline(intercept = 1, slope = 1, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") + geom_path(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(data = default_calls, size = 3.2) + scale_x_reverse() + scale_colour_ml() + coord_equal() + labs(x = "Specificity", y = "Sensitivity", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ROC curves of the two models' out-of-fold probabilities, showing sensitivity against specificity at every threshold. The dashed diagonal is ranking at random. The points mark the default threshold of 0.5, high on sensitivity and low on specificity. The forest's curve, with a ROC AUC of 0.723, lies above logistic regression's, at 0.671.](classification-metrics_files/figure-html/fig-roc-1.png){#fig-roc fig-alt='A plot of sensitivity from 0 to 1 against specificity running from 1 on the left to 0 on the right, with a dashed diagonal from the bottom left to the top right. Two curves rise from the bottom left corner to the top right corner, both above the diagonal. The orange curve, the random forest, lies above the blue one, logistic regression, along most of its length. A point on each curve marks the threshold of 0.5, both near the top right corner, logistic regression at specificity 0.07 and the forest at 0.22.' width=1120} ::: ::: ::: The forest's ROC AUC is 0.723, and logistic regression's 0.671: in about 72 of 100 pairs of a station with the species and one without, the forest gives the station with the species the higher probability. Its curve lies above the other along most of its length, so whatever threshold is chosen, the forest can reach the same sensitivity with fewer false alarms. The points show why the first part made the two models look so alike: 0.5 sits near the top right corner, where the curves are closest. ### Log loss rewards probabilities that are spread out and calibrated ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} probability_scores <- predictions |> summarise(`log loss` = mn_log_loss_vec(present, probability), lowest = min(probability), highest = max(probability), .by = model) probability_scores |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | log loss| lowest| highest| |:----------------------------|--------:|------:|-------:| |Predicting the share present | 0.535| 0.766| 0.784| |Logistic regression | 0.503| 0.271| 0.958| |Random forest | 0.472| 0.091| 0.988|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} probability_scores = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False) .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "log loss": log_loss(g.present, g.probability), "lowest": g.probability.min(), "highest": g.probability.max(), }), include_groups=False) .reset_index()) probability_scores.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | log loss | lowest | highest | |:-----------------------------|-----------:|---------:|----------:| | Predicting the share present | 0.535 | 0.764 | 0.786 | | Logistic regression | 0.513 | 0.303 | 0.963 | | Random forest | 0.486 | 0.082 | 0.988 | ::: ::: ::: A **calibration plot** checks the second half of what log loss rewards. It sorts each model's stations by their predicted probability into eight groups of 100, and plots each group's average probability against the share of its stations where the species was caught. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(calibration, aes(predicted, observed, colour = model)) + geom_abline(colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 2.8) + annotate("point", x = share_present, y = share_present, shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 1.6, colour = "grey45") + scale_colour_ml() + coord_equal(xlim = c(0.3, 1), ylim = c(0.3, 1)) + labs(x = "Average predicted probability", y = "Share with the species", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Calibration of the two models' out-of-fold probabilities, in eight groups of 100 stations each. Points on the dashed diagonal mean the probabilities can be read as chances. The grey cross is predicting the share present, which gives every station the same probability. Both models stay close to the diagonal; the forest's groups spread from 0.40 to 0.96, wider than logistic regression's.](classification-metrics_files/figure-html/fig-calibration-1.png){#fig-calibration fig-alt='A plot of the share of stations with the species against the average predicted probability, both from 0.3 to 1, with a dashed diagonal. Eight blue points for logistic regression run from 0.54 to 0.93 along the diagonal, a little above or below it. Eight orange points for the random forest run further, from 0.40 to 0.96, also close to the diagonal. A single grey cross for predicting the share present sits on the diagonal at 0.78.' width=1120} ::: ::: ::: Both models' groups stay close to the diagonal, so their probabilities can be read as chances. Predicting the share present is calibrated too: it says 0.78 everywhere, and the species was caught at 78% of the stations. What it lacks is spread, and log loss charges it the most, at 0.535. Logistic regression lowers that to 0.503 and the forest to 0.472, 12% below the rule. The forest gains by spreading its probabilities further, from 0.09 to 0.99 against logistic regression's 0.27 to 0.96, while staying calibrated. The spread that lowers its log loss is the same that gave it the higher ROC AUC. Here the three kinds of measure agree on the order of the models. The diagram above shows that they need not. ## Balanced accuracy scores calls, ROC AUC rankings and log loss chances When the calls drive the work, at a threshold already chosen from what each mistake costs, report measures of the calls, and choose balanced accuracy or MCC unless the true absences really do not matter. To compare models before the threshold is chosen, report ROC AUC. When the probabilities themselves are used, as on a map of the chance of finding the species or when they are added up into an expected number of occupied stations, report log loss and check a calibration plot. ROC AUC cannot tell whether a 0.8 means 8 in 10. [Choosing measures that match the objective](choosing-a-metric.qmd) takes this further. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Presence can be scored on the **calls** at one threshold, on the **ranking** the probabilities make, or on the **probabilities** themselves. A model can do well on one and poorly on another. - **F1** never counts the true absences. With the species at 78% of stations, calling every station present scored an F1 of 0.873, within 0.002 of both models. **Balanced accuracy** and **MCC** count every cell and told the models apart. - **ROC AUC** is the area under the curve of sensitivity against specificity: the share of pairs, one station with the species and one without, ranked the right way round. It is 0.5 for ranking at random, and it ignores how high or low the probabilities are. - **Log loss** rewards probabilities that are both spread out and **calibrated**. A calibration plot shows whether a predicted 0.8 means 8 in 10. - yardstick treats the first level of the outcome as the event. Check the levels before trusting any of these measures. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add a fourth model: logistic regression with `step_upsample(present)` from the `themis` package at the end of its recipe, as in [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd). Predict first: does its ROC AUC or its log loss move more? 2. Score the three models on `rare_species` instead of `present`. How does the F1 of predicting the share present change when the species is rare?
